sections.label: Section 1: Finding and Describing Local Art Forms

children.label: 1A: Finding Local Genres
children.guidance: A 'genre' is a kind of song, poem, story, or chant your people use. List the ones people enjoy, understand, and can still make and perform today.

children.label: List the kinds of songs, poems, stories, and chants your people use. Choose ones that people understand, enjoy, and can still create and perform today (for listening, singing, reading, or performing).
Genres you have found so far
children.footnote: These prompts are only a few of many ideas for finding genres; see pages 67-69 of the CLAT Companion for more. For more on why local genres matter, see 'Why Consider Local Genres in Translation?' (Frost 2024).

children.label: People to ask (for example: leaders, teachers, artists, mothers)

children.label: 1C: Matching the Psalm to a Genre

Which genre or genres fit this psalm's message and purpose? What works well? What problems might there be (who uses it, when, or what it reminds people of), and how could you handle them? (Write your final choices in Psalm Genre Choice.)

xref.label: write your choices in Psalm Genre Choice

children.label: 2A: How This Genre Makes Things Stand Out

How does this genre make its most important part stand out? Think of genres you know and give examples. For example: by where it is placed; by a repeated line (a refrain); by repeating words; by surprising the listener; by strong feeling; or by packing many strong features together.
How does it make the second-most important parts stand out?
What tells the listener that the high point has arrived?
children.footnote: This may overlap with the most important material above. If you have not done the detailed study in Section 3 yet, make a note to come back and add to this answer later.

children.label: How does the genre build up to its most beautiful or powerful moment, the part people will remember most?
children.footnote: Example: in Psalm 67, the middle verse is marked as special in several ways. This draws attention to the peoples of the world, and it sets up the main point of the psalm: that the ends of the earth will fear God.

children.label: 2B: The Parts (Sections) of This Genre
How is this genre ordered from start to finish? What usually comes first, next, and last?
What are the main parts of a full performance? (How many parts, and what is each part for?)
children.footnote: Some genres flow straight through from start to finish and do not have clear separate parts.

children.label: How do the parts relate to each other? (For example: repeated, opposite, or a changed version of another part.)
If there is music, how do the parts fit the music? (For example: the same or a different tune for each line; a high point in the music that you can expect.)
If different people or characters take part, which person performs which lines or parts?
What tells the listener that one part has ended and a new one has started? (For example: the topic, the mood, the rhythm or sound, who is speaking, the instruments, or the way the voice sounds.)
What usually marks the beginning, the middle, and the end, both of the whole genre and of each part?
children.footnote: Examples: expected words, content, set phrases, performance features, pauses or timing, or a change in the space, the objects, or the people taking part. See Section 3 for more ideas.

sections.label: Section 3: The Genre's Style and Details

children.label: 3A: How This Genre Uses Words

Does this genre use set phrases or sayings? Where in the piece do they come? (For example, a saying like 'better to be poor and honest than rich and cruel.') Are some words repeated at the start of lines? Are names, or words like 'no' and 'not', used in special ways?
Does this genre play with words? (For example: words that sound alike, words with two meanings, jokes made with words, or two opposite ideas put side by side.)
What kind of language does this genre use? (For example: a special dialect or accent; polite, normal, or everyday speech; special or old words; borrowed words; rare words.)

Does this genre build its lines in special ways? (For example: saying the same thing twice in different words; a sentence that runs over into the next line; a question that does not need an answer; or leaving out a word that the listener already understands.)
Special word features to keep in the translation

columns.label: What you noticed
How fixed is it?

children.label: 3B: How the Text Is Put Together (Discourse)
Does the point of view change through the genre? (For example: is there a narrator? Does the speaker change? Does the person being spoken to change?)

How are people named in this genre? The first time someone is mentioned, how are they named? After that, do they use a short name, a word like 'he' or 'she', or no name at all? How does the listener know who is being talked about? (For example: first 'the old chief came'; after that, just 'he said'.)

How are action words (verbs) used? Do some carry the main story while others give background detail? Are some verb forms used only in certain parts (for example, one form for the main events and another for side comments)?
Does the genre quote people's exact words, or report them? Are there small words used again and again (for example, a word that means 'thus' or 'look!')?
3C: The Sounds of This Genre
How is the rhythm made? (For example: the number of beats or syllables in each line; a steady pulse you can feel; chanting.)
Does it use rhyme at the ends? (between words, between lines, or between verses?)
Are there other matching sounds? (For example: words that start with the same sound; the same vowel sound repeated; the same consonant sound repeated.) Where do they come, and how?
Does it use sounds that carry no meaning, like 'la-la-la' or 'hey'? Where do they appear, and what are they for?
Does it use words that imitate sounds or actions? (For example: 'boom' or 'splash', or a word that paints how something moves.)
If your language uses tones, how do the tones work together with the rhythm and the matching sounds above?
3D: Picture-Language (Figurative Language)
What picture-language does this genre use? Note whether it is used, and how (where in the piece, about what topics, alone or in groups).

columns.label: Type

options.label: A name for something closely linked to it (like 'the crown' for the king)
Personification (gives human traits to a thing)
Symbolism (a thing stands for an idea)
A gentle word for something hard to say
Stereotype (a fixed image of a group)
Idiom (a saying whose meaning is not its plain words)

columns.label: Is it used, and how?

children.label: What other ways does this genre use to paint pictures in the mind?
3E: How This Genre Is Performed

How is the voice used? (For example: the rise and fall of the sound; fast or slow; clear or soft sounds; loud or quiet; the quality of the voice, such as rough, smooth, nasal, or breathy; how strong it is.) Say why it matters, what it does, how it changes through the piece, and the key places.
How does movement add to it? (body positions, gestures, facial expressions)
If your language uses tones, how do the tones work together with the voice features above?
3F: Other Things You Notice
Word order: is the order of the doer, the action, and the thing fixed? When does it change? Where in the line does a new idea (something the listener has not heard yet) usually appear?
How are parts joined together? (For example: repeating the last idea of one part at the start of the next, so the listener can follow.)
Are smaller forms placed inside this genre? (For example: a riddle or a proverb.) Which kind, and where?
What is repeated? (words, phrases, the shape of the text, themes, characters, or picture-language?)
How packed is it? (How much repetition? How much new information in each line? How fast do new ideas come?)
Anything else about this genre that does not fit the groups above?

Write your style findings into the Psalm Notes: The Small Details (in Section 0).
